newsitem.title: SPAIN: Explosion in suspected ETA hideaway in Spain.
newsitem.headline: Explosion in suspected ETA hideaway in Spain.

text.p: A loud explosion ripped through an apartment believed to be a hideaway for the Basque guerrilla group ETA on Thursday, only days after the separatist rebels killed a young politician.

With Spain still seething with anger over the murder of town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco, police reported a blast possibly triggered by bomb-making materials stored in an ETA "safe house" in the Basque town of Durango.
The people in the apartment fled, and police blanketed the area and set up roadblocks in the search for suspects.
Gestoras Pro Amnistia, a human rights group that lobbies for better conditions for ETA prisoners, said one man was arrested. This could not be officially confirmed.
Police said they found an arsenal of weapons inside the apartment, including grenades and bomb parts. Officials said no one was injured.
The massive police response to the explosion reflected the sense of unease that has pervaded the Basque country of northern Spain since Blanco's kidnapping and murder.

Millions of people have taken to the streets throughout Spain to express their outrage. In some cases, angry crowds have attacked ETA sympathisers. Authorities have expressed fears that the rebels may retaliate by stepping up their attacks.
In the Basque city of San Sebastian, officials have been bracing for a demonstration planned for Saturday by ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna.

The Basque regional government on Wednesday banned the protest for fear it would ignite more violence. Herri Batasuna said on Thursday it had filed an appeal in local court but would call off the rally if the ban was upheld.
"There's no demonstration on Saturday unless the judge says that it is legal," Herri Batasuna leader Floren Aoiz told reporters. A ruling was expected on Friday.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and other Spanish politicial leaders have branded Herri Batasuna "accomplices" to murder and have sought to isolate it. But leaders of the radical political party claim they are being targeted for a "political lynching".
Adding its voice to the outcry against ETA, Spain's parliament condemned the guerrillas for Blanco's killing and vowed to take action to stop Basque separatist violence.

Blanco, 29, was kidnapped last Thursday by rebels demanding the transfer of 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the autonomous Basque region within 48 hours. The government refused, and ETA shot him twice in the head on Saturday. He died 12 hours later.

Spaniards, shocked by the killing of such an ordinary low-level functionary, have mounted huge street protests against ETA. The government estimates that six million people have demonstrated across the country since Blanco's death.
Basques, once intimidated by the radical separatists, have been emboldened by the nationwide condemnation. ETA has killed nearly 800 people in its violent struggle for an independent Basque homeland.
Aznar's government has promised a crackdown on ETA and is formulating tougher legislation to combat terrorism. He told parliament it was its duty "to carry out the response that society demands".

However, too tough a crackdown could play into the hands of ETA by generating public sympathy for its claims that the government violates human rights, analysts say. ETA has already shown its defiance by threatening a second Basque town councillor with death.
